synopsis: One juror refuses to vote guilty, and a sweltering afternoon of deliberation turns into a slow dismantling of everything the other eleven took for granted. Almost entirely one room, one table and twelve men, and it never once feels stagey.

A free Black musician in 1840s New York is drugged, sold south, and spends over a decade on Louisiana plantations that have no interest in his papers. McQueen holds shots long past the point of comfort, which is the argument rather than a flourish.

Aboard a ship bound for Jupiter, two astronauts and the computer that runs everything drift towards a confrontation neither was briefed on, bookended by prehistory and something stranger. More an argument about evolution than a story, and the silences carry most of it.

The head writer of a flailing New York sketch show juggles a volatile star, a needy cast and a corporate boss who has decided to mentor her whether she likes it or not. Jokes arrive faster than most comedies attempt, and roughly nine in ten land.

A gleeful young thug in a near-future Britain leads his gang through a spree of violence, then submits to a state programme that promises to cure him of the urge. Kubrick never lets you off the hook about whose company you were enjoying.

Built to love and placed with a grieving couple, a robot child is abandoned in the woods and sets out to find a way of becoming real. Spielberg finishing Kubrick's project yields a colder, sadder fairy tale than either would have made alone.

A Tehran couple split over whether to leave the country, and the carer hired to look after the husband's father becomes the centre of a dispute neither family can afford to lose. Farhadi builds moral pressure out of nothing but conflicting, plausible accounts.

In 1967 Minnesota, a physics professor watches his marriage, his tenure case and his health unravel at once, and goes looking for a rabbi who can tell him why. The Coens at their driest, staging the book of Job as suburban farce.

A screenwriter hired to adapt a book about orchid hunting cannot find the story in it, so he writes himself into the script, along with his fictional twin brother. A film about its own impossibility that eventually surrenders to plot, on purpose and with a smirk.

Sent downtown for a late date, a bored word processor spends the rest of the night unable to get home, hounded by nearly everyone he meets. Scorsese doing paranoid farce, tight and mean and over before the idea wears thin.

A local newspaper journalist in a small English town, wrecked by his wife's death, decides that saying whatever he likes to whoever he likes is a kind of superpower. Swings hard between real grief and Gervais enjoying his own bluntness, often in the same scene.

Twenty years on, a woman revisits camcorder footage of a package holiday in Turkey with her young father, reading it for everything she was too small to see. Devastating by accumulation rather than incident, and Mescal plays the gaps rather than the lines.

In a rebuilt Tokyo of biker gangs and buried military projects, a teenager injured in a crash develops powers the state has spent decades trying to contain. The animation is still astonishing; the plot compresses a much longer manga and shows the seams.

A directionless Tokyo gamer and his two friends find the city emptied of people and themselves conscripted into lethal games scored by playing cards, on visas that expire. Sharper about its puzzles than most of the genre, weakest whenever it stops to explain itself.

The crew of a commercial towing ship answer a distress signal on an empty moon and carry something back aboard with them. Built like a haunted house with the corridors welded shut, and its restraint about showing the creature has never been bettered.

Recovered after decades adrift, the sole survivor of the first encounter returns to the now-colonised moon with a squad of marines who are certain this will be straightforward. Cameron swaps dread for sustained tension and gets away with it.

Two Washington Post reporters pull at a break-in at Democratic headquarters and find the thread runs all the way into the White House. Almost entirely phone calls, door-knocks and typing, which turns out to be the most gripping possible way to film it.

An elderly Parisian music teacher cares for his wife in their flat after a stroke leaves her failing faster than either of them prepared for. Haneke's usual coldness serves tenderness for once, and the refusal to leave the apartment is what makes it unbearable.

Sent to live with a grandmother he barely knows, a teenager finds her southern Californian household is a surf-and-rob crime family run on charm and threat. Trades the chill of the Australian film it came from for sun, muscle and soap, and is more fun for it.

An army captain travels upriver into Cambodia under orders to find and kill a decorated colonel who has set himself up as a god. The war recedes into hallucination the further the boat goes, and the production's own chaos is visible in the frame.

A spy agency staffed almost entirely by narcissists sends its best and worst field agent on missions that collapse into arguments with his mother, who runs the place. The dialogue overlaps and doubles back at a speed that rewards a second viewing.

When a fraud indictment removes its patriarch, a wealthy Californian property family is left to the one competent son, who holds them together against his better judgement. Dense with callbacks and running jokes that pay off seasons later; the first three runs are the ones.

A junior stargazing convention in a 1955 desert town is interrupted by an event that puts everyone under quarantine, all of it framed as a broadcast about a play. Anderson's most nested construction, which either moves you or keeps you at arm's length.

With no money and less of a plan, a Princeton dropout manages his cousin's rap career, drifting through a city that keeps handing the pair of them strange encounters. Abandons its plot for standalone nightmares whenever it feels like it, and those are the best episodes.

A struggling comedian pulls a free pint for a woman in distress and spends years unable to extract himself from the stalking that follows, or from what it exposes in him. Adapted by the man it happened to, which is both its force and its problem.

Silent-era Hollywood at full tilt, followed through a studio fixer, a fading star and an actress on the way up, until the arrival of sound starts shedding people. Three hours of excess about excess; exhausting by design, and about half of it lands.

Fresh out of prison, a career thief arrives in a small Pennsylvania town, assumes the identity of its incoming sheriff, and keeps the badge while settling scores of his own. Trashy in the best sense, with fight scenes choreographed far better than the show required.

A depressed hitman follows a mark into an acting class in Los Angeles and decides he would rather be an actor, with no plan at all for leaving the first job. Gets darker every season until the comedy is doing something quite different.

Duelling, deserting and gambling his way into the English aristocracy, an eighteenth-century Irish chancer discovers that holding a position is far harder than taking one. Shot by candlelight at a pace that dares you to leave, with all the cruelty carried by the narration.

A New York playwright with a social conscience is hired to write a wrestling picture for a studio and checks into a Los Angeles hotel that appears to be sweating. Begins as Hollywood satire, then curdles into something the Coens decline to explain.

A billionaire orphan trains abroad with a shadowy order of vigilantes, then returns to a Gotham owned by mobsters and corrupt police with a costume and a plan. The first superhero film to take fear seriously as a subject, and still the most grounded of Nolan's three.

The last fifty thousand humans flee across space in a ragtag convoy after a machine race annihilates their colonies, hunted by enemies who now look exactly like them. Uses its premise to argue about torture, occupation and elections rather than spaceships, and mostly wins the argument.

Two strangers turn a car park confrontation into a campaign of mutual ruin that takes in their families, jobs and churches. An anthology, each season a fresh grudge with a new cast, built on the idea that rage is mostly despair with somewhere to go.

A frustrated puppeteer takes a filing job on a half-height office floor and finds a portal that drops anyone into the head of the actor John Malkovich for fifteen minutes. Kaufman's debut script is absurd in premise and ruthless about vanity, desire and who gets to be someone else.

Between auditions for parts she does not want, a jobbing Los Angeles actor raises three daughters alone and manages her own difficult ageing mother. Built from fragments rather than plots, and better for it, with domestic detail that stays unsentimental about how little thanks any of it gets.

A man in postwar Rome lands a job that requires a bicycle, has it stolen on the first morning, and spends the day combing the city for it with his small son. Neorealism at its plainest and most devastating, with the streets and the non-actors doing half the work.

Three mothers at an affluent Monterey primary school are drawn together by playground politics, a custody feud and a violence none of them will name. Plays as glossy soap and works as one, while being far sharper about domestic abuse than the beach houses suggest.

The respectable children of a Florida Keys hotel family close ranks when their eldest brother comes home and starts pulling at everything they have buried. The first season is a humid, tightly wound slow burn; the two that follow never quite find the same shape.

Three probationary officers join a response unit in Belfast, where every routine call runs through decades of local history and no uniform reads as neutral. The procedural bones are ordinary; what makes it is the political weather, and the question of who will talk to police at all.

Atlantic City's treasurer runs bootlegging, patronage and most of the county from behind a public servant's smile as Prohibition opens for business. Lavish and deliberate, assembled more as a period portrait of American corruption than as a gangster thriller, though the gangsters are there.

Four detectives in four eras, Victorian London, the Blitz, the present and a future city, each find the same naked corpse at the same East End address. A puzzle box that earns its explanation, keeping four period dramas distinct while locking them together.

A washed-up sitcom star, who happens to be a horse, tries to relaunch a career from his Hollywood mansion while the people around him absorb the damage. Begins as an animal-pun comedy and becomes one of television's most exact accounts of depression and self-sabotage.

In the late-Seventies San Fernando Valley, a porn director takes up a teenage dishwasher with one obvious asset and builds him into a star. Anderson catches the industry's makeshift-family warmth in the first half, then lets the Eighties and cocaine take it apart.

A US border patrol agent and his Mexican-American neighbour needle each other across the fence line of a desert suburb where the demographics keep shifting. A Fox animated satire with Family Guy's joke rhythms that tried to run immigration politics as a weekly gag engine; one season was all it got.

On the run after shooting a policeman, a small-time Paris car thief chases an unpaid debt and tries to talk an American student selling newspapers into leaving with him. The jump cuts and the shrugging amorality made the New Wave's opening statement, and it is still looser than most films since.

An insurance lawyer is handed the defence of a Soviet spy in Cold War Brooklyn, then sent to a divided Berlin to trade him for a downed American pilot. Spielberg at his most procedural, and Rylance underplays so far that he walks off with the film.

The best detective in a Brooklyn precinct is a gifted man-child, and his new commanding officer is a rigidly formal captain unimpressed by talent without discipline. Joke-dense workplace comedy with a genuinely warm ensemble, though its cheerful vision of policing aged into a position it only half-acknowledged.

Two gym employees find a disc of a sacked CIA analyst's memoir on the changing-room floor and decide someone will pay to get it back. The Coens in farce mode, letting vain idiots collide while the intelligence service gives up trying to explain what happened.

A young aspiring writer reconnects with a girl from his old village, then meets the wealthy, unreadable man she comes back from a trip with, and slowly convinces himself something is wrong. Adapted from Murakami into class resentment and heat haze; the ambiguity is the point, so expect no receipts.

The agents at a Paris talent firm scramble to keep their film-star clients, and the agency itself, from falling apart after the founder dies. French stars send themselves up as guests each week, but the real pleasure is the office, which is bruising and affectionate in equal measure.

Nurses and nuns from an East End convent deliver babies across the tenements of Poplar in the 1950s and 60s, on bicycles, in homes with no hot water. Much tougher than its Sunday-evening slot implies, working steadily through abortion, thalidomide and race in postwar Britain.

A decent priest in a coastal Irish parish is told in confession that he will be killed in a week for another cleric's crimes, and carries on with his rounds regardless. Gleeson is extraordinary, and the black comedy never blunts the film's anger at the Church.

In Vichy-controlled Morocco, the owner of a nightclub holds two stolen letters of transit and no politics at all, until his former lover walks in with her Resistance-leader husband. A studio picture made fast that happens to get everything right, with wartime urgency that is real rather than retrospective.

A gifted handicapper is installed to run a mob-financed Las Vegas casino, and his hustler wife and volatile enforcer friend grind the operation into the ground. Scorsese narrating a business from the inside out, colder and more bureaucratic than Goodfellas, and three hours long on purpose.

Before he turns twenty a runaway passes millions in bad cheques across America, posing as an airline pilot, a doctor and a lawyer while a dogged FBI fraud agent closes in. Spielberg's lightest film, though the caper keeps circling back to a boy trying to reassemble his parents' marriage.

Regulars drink their evenings away in a Boston basement bar run by a retired ballplayer, whose long argument with a graduate-student waitress becomes the house sport. The template for the American ensemble sitcom, with writing that takes its laughs from character rather than premise.

A sheltered, religiously raised shop assistant on a Tower Hamlets estate decides she is finished with virginity and has no idea how to go about it. Coel's first series is filthy, fast and physically fearless, with a real strain of loneliness running under the farce.

In Thirties Los Angeles a private detective takes a routine adultery job and finds himself inside the question of who owns the city's water. Perfectly built noir whose real subject is power no investigation can reach, and it closes on one of the bleakest endings the studios ever allowed.

Two lovesick Hong Kong policemen drift through a late-night food stall and a borrowed apartment in two loosely linked stories, while the women they fixate on get on with their own plans. Shot quickly between larger projects, and the looseness is exactly why it still feels alive.

A newspaper tycoon dies alone in his unfinished palace, and a reporter works through everyone who knew him trying to decide what his last word meant. The formal invention still reads clearly, deep focus and fractured chronology, but what holds is the portrait of a man who buys company.

Two boys grow up in a Rio housing project across the sixties and seventies, one drifting towards a camera and the other towards a gun, as the drug trade hardens around them. The kinetic editing is famous, but what lasts is the patient bookkeeping of how children become soldiers.

An Indiana power-line worker sees something in the sky and starts compulsively sculpting a mountain shape he cannot explain, while scientists trace repeating signals across the globe. Spielberg's most generous film about obsession, and the rare first-contact story that treats wonder itself as the whole point.

Born hearing into a deaf family, a teenager interprets for their struggling fishing business until the school choir puts those duties on a collision course with her own voice. Sentimental by design, but the deaf cast play it straight and one sequence that drops the sound entirely justifies the film.

Over one night in Los Angeles, a cab driver is commandeered by a well-dressed passenger with five stops to make, and works out too late what the names on the list have in common. Shot on early digital that makes the city glow sodium-orange; Mann's best argument that a thriller can be a mood piece.

A pizza delivery man is shot dead in south London and a detective inspector pulls the thread through immigration detention, an army barracks and Westminster. A four-part state-of-the-nation piece from David Hare that cares far more about who Britain lets in than about whodunnit.

Occupied Los Angeles is walled into blocs under an unseen alien authority, and a former FBI agent takes a collaborator's job to reach the son trapped outside. Strongest as a study of collaboration and resistance under any occupation; the aliens are almost beside the point.

A Belarusian boy digs up a rifle and joins the partisans in 1943, then walks through what the German reprisal squads leave behind. Klimov films atrocity without catharsis, and the boy's face ageing across two hours is the hardest thing any war film has put on screen.

Seven misfits at a shabby Colorado community college form a study group none of them can leave, convened by a disbarred lawyer who only joined to chat up a classmate. The concept episodes — paintball, stop-motion, a clip show of things that never happened — mostly land, and the cast sells the sentiment underneath.

Returning from a fatal accident on the space station, an astronaut finds her flat, her daughter and her marriage subtly wrong, and nobody willing to check the discrepancies. Beautiful cold-weather dread, well acted by Rapace, that sets up rather more than its ending manages to pay off.

A drifter draws two years on a Florida chain gang for decapitating parking meters, and declines, politely and repeatedly, to be broken by any of it. Newman turned the charm down rather than up, and the film is sharper about a crowd needing a martyr than about the martyr.

In a Mexico City antiques shop, a dealer finds a gilded clockwork scarab hidden inside a statue and is bitten into a slow, undignified immortality that a dying industrialist wants for himself. Del Toro's debut already carries the whole toolkit: Catholic imagery, tender monsters, and machinery you can hear ticking.

A master swordsman gives up his legendary blade, it is stolen within a night, and the theft drags into the open what he and a fellow warrior have spent years refusing to say. The wire work is weightless and lovely, but the film is really a chamber drama about restraint.

Larry David plays a version of himself who cannot let a minor social infraction go, and each episode tightens a dozen small grievances into one appalling knot. Improvised from outlines rather than scripted, which is exactly why the cringe lands harder than written jokes could.

Abducted by a masked man, a Chicago physics lecturer wakes into a version of his life where he took the career and lost the family. Genuinely thoughtful about roads not taken for its first half, then settles into a chase; Edgerton holds the whole thing together.

A lawless gold camp in the Dakota hills accretes into a town, watched over by a saloon owner whose cruelty doubles as civic planning. Milch wrote it in filthy iambic pentameter, and it remains the only western that treats profanity as poetry rather than colour.

When a teenage boy is accused of killing a classmate, his father, the assistant district attorney first assigned the case, keeps investigating long after he has any business doing so. Deliberate to the point of slow, but honest about parents who settle on what they believe first.

In a rusting post-apocalyptic tenement above a butcher's shop, the landlord hires handymen he has no intention of paying in money, and the latest one falls for his daughter. Jeunet and Caro's sepia slapstick runs on rhythm: a squeaking bedspring becomes an entire orchestrated set piece.

Four schoolgirls and one bewildered English boy negotiate exams, crushes and Catholic school in nineties Derry, with the Troubles as background noise their parents have stopped hearing. Very funny about teenage self-absorption, and it drops the historical weight in only when it has earned it.

Two men sweep Essex fields with metal detectors, hunting Saxon gold and turning up ring pulls, while the lives they are avoiding quietly ask for attention. Crook writes comedy with almost no jokes per minute and a startling amount of grace; the hedgerows and birdsong do half the work.

In the antebellum South, a freed slave partners with a German bounty hunter and talks his way onto a Mississippi plantation to buy back his wife. Tarantino's most purely satisfying revenge structure, though it runs long and Waltz's charm carries stretches the script does not.

A blonde hair on her husband's scarf sends a GP in a comfortable commuter town investigating her own marriage with the cold thoroughness of a diagnosis. Suranne Jones is ferocious, and the first series is a superb study of a woman repeatedly told she is imagining it.

An alien with two hearts travels time and space in a battered police box, picks up a human companion who needs one, and regenerates into a new face whenever the lead actor leaves. The revival's tonal range is the whole appeal: silly, then frightening, then abruptly sad, often inside one episode.

Across the Russian Revolution and the civil war that follows, a physician and poet is pulled between his wife and a woman he keeps meeting by accident. Lean shoots the ice and the crowds magnificently, but the politics stay decorative and the romance is a chilly thing at its centre.

A first-time robber holds up a Brooklyn bank on a sweltering August afternoon, finds the money is not there, and watches the pavement outside fill with police, news crews and a crowd picking sides. Lumet lets it sprawl and improvise until the farce curdles into something sadder.

Three adult children are raised inside a walled compound on invented vocabulary and staged threats, with a single outsider admitted on a strict schedule. Lanthimos's deadpan is at its most clinical here, and it is funny in a way that leaves you unsure you should have laughed.

An insurance salesman is talked into killing a client's husband by the client's wife, and the claims investigator he most admires starts pulling at the policy. Wilder and Chandler wrote dialogue so hard-boiled it nearly tips over, and the rest of the genre took its shape from here.

The last days in the Berlin bunker, seen largely through a young secretary who typed for Hitler and had no idea what she would spend her life explaining. Ganz plays him as a physically failing man rather than a symbol, which is precisely why the film unsettles.

An English earl with no son faces losing the estate to a distant middle-class cousin, while the household below stairs runs its own hierarchy with equal seriousness. Comfort viewing built on real craft, and the Dowager Countess gets lines far better than the plotting deserves.

Grieving his wife, a stage actor directs a multilingual Chekhov production in Hiroshima and is assigned a young woman to drive his red Saab between the theatre and his lodgings. Three hours that never drag, about grief conducted in cars and rehearsal rooms instead of speeches.

The exiled heir joins the Fremen in the deep desert, learns to ride the worms, and takes up a prophecy he knows was planted centuries earlier to be used. Villeneuve delivers the spectacle while keeping Herbert's warning intact: this is a messiah story told as a horror story.

Three hundred thousand men wait on a French beach for boats that may not come, the story told across a stone mole, a small civilian yacht and a Spitfire's fuel gauge. Nolan strips out backstory almost entirely and lets sound design and interlocking clocks do the work of character.

A lonely suburban boy hides a stranded alien in his bedroom cupboard and feeds him sweets while government men close in on the neighbourhood. Spielberg shoots almost everything at child height, which is why the sentiment lands rather than cloys.

Scholarship pupils from a collapsed state school arrive at Spain's most exclusive academy, and within a term someone is dead and everyone is lying to the police. The murder framing is mostly scaffolding for a soapy, frank ensemble drama that swaps out half its cast every couple of series.

A young Oxford detective constable with an unfinished degree and a taste for opera works murders under a gruff inspector who teaches him how policing actually gets done. A prequel that justifies itself by being about the 1960s changing around its hero rather than about Morse trivia.

In a rented film, a withdrawn history lecturer spots his exact double, tracks the man down, and finds the resemblance goes further than either of them can stand. Villeneuve's smallest and strangest picture: an anxiety dream about fidelity and repetition, shot the colour of nicotine, that withholds any tidy explanation.

After a break-up, a withdrawn man pays a clinic to erase his girlfriend from his memory, then changes his mind midway through the procedure and tries to hide her inside his own head. Gondry's in-camera tricks keep it tactile, and Carrey has never been better used.

A background artist with no lines schemes for a speaking part while famous people play grotesque versions of themselves on the sets around him. Funnier about humiliation than The Office was, and it ends on one of the bleakest notes British comedy has managed.

Rattled by his wife's confession of a fantasy, a Manhattan doctor spends two nights wandering the city and talks his way into a masked ritual he has no business attending. Kubrick's last film is a marriage drama disguised as an erotic thriller, and far funnier and sadder than its reputation.

A reformed chicken thief takes one last run at three vicious farmers and brings the whole valley's animal population down on itself. Anderson's stop-motion fur twitches frame by frame, and the Dahl misanthropy survives the whimsy better than it had any right to.

Drowning in debt, a Minnesota car salesman hires two men to kidnap his own wife, and a pregnant police chief follows the resulting bodies back up the road. The Coens' funniest film about decency, and the only one where ordinary politeness is the moral centre.

Torquay's least hospitable hotelier abuses his guests, his staff and his wife while every small deception collapses into a larger one. Twelve episodes, no filler, and a farce engine built so precisely that the timing still holds fifty years on.

An insomniac office drone falls in with a soap salesman who preaches destruction, and the basement brawls they start spread into something organised. Fincher's satire of consumer masculinity is routinely mistaken for an endorsement, which is either its flaw or the whole joke.

Smugglers on a beaten-up transport ship take dodgy jobs on the frontier of a settled solar system, carrying two passengers the authorities badly want back. A western first and science fiction second, cancelled after fourteen episodes, which is why its reputation so far outgrew its run.

The years of test flights, bereavement and committee rooms that carry one taciturn engineer from the Mojave to the Sea of Tranquility. Chazelle shoots space travel as violent, rattling manual labour, and keeps the man himself almost unreachable.

A jobless would-be writer starts trailing strangers around London for material and is drawn into burglary by one of them, a man who breaks in to disturb people rather than to profit. Nolan's shoestring debut already has the shuffled chronology and the con-trick structure he would spend decades refining.

An apprentice dancer in New York loses her flat, her best friend and any clear sense of a career, and keeps insisting she is doing fine. Shot in black and white and played with real physical comedy by Gerwig, it is generous about failure without pretending it does not sting.

Seattle's fussiest radio psychiatrist takes in his blue-collar ex-cop father and spars with an even fussier brother over sherry, opera tickets and wounded pride. A sitcom built on farce and class snobbery that wrote better sentences than almost anything else on American television.

Six twenty-somethings in improbably large Manhattan flats work bad jobs, date badly and spend most of a decade on the same coffee-shop sofa. The joke rhythm is machine-tooled and the cast chemistry is real, even where the writing has aged into something you have to talk around.

An FBI agent, a decommissioned mad scientist and his con-artist son investigate impossible crimes that turn out to be symptoms of a much larger structural problem. It begins as a case-of-the-week knock-off and becomes one of the most committed serialised science-fiction shows American network television made.

Marine recruits are broken down by a drill instructor on Parris Island, then dispatched to Vietnam and the rubble of Hue. Two films bolted together, and the long argument over whether the second half matches the first is the most interesting thing about it.

A pizza delivery boy is frozen on New Year's Eve 1999 and wakes a thousand years later to work for a delivery company run by his senile descendant. Sharper on actual science than any cartoon needs to be, and prone to ambushing you with an episode that is quietly devastating.

Noble houses scheme, marry and butcher one another for a continent's throne while something far worse gathers beyond the northern wall. Superb at political consequence for as long as it had books beneath it; the later seasons move faster than their own logic can support.

A Yorkshire landowner in the 1830s runs her own coal pits, rebuilds a crumbling estate and courts a wealthy neighbour, recording all of it in a coded diary. Wainwright's script talks straight to camera and treats Anne Lister as a businesswoman first, which is what makes the romance work.

Sent to London to find the brother he was told was dead, a Tokyo detective walks into a yakuza dispute that has already crossed continents. A crime drama that keeps breaking into animation, split screens and dance, and somehow stays tender rather than showy.

A wife vanishes from a Missouri house on the morning of her fifth anniversary, and her husband's flat affect in front of the cameras turns the search into a national trial. Fincher and Flynn are really making a film about performing a marriage for an audience.

Brooklyn, and a boy starts running errands for the local crew, then spends thirty years inside the mob on easy money, casual violence and eventually cocaine. Scorsese makes the life look wonderful for an hour precisely so the decline registers as a physical shock.

A teenage boy and his small sister are orphaned in the firebombing of Kobe and try to survive the last months of the war on their own. Takahata refuses both sentiment and sermon, and it is as devastating as animation gets.

Debris destroys a shuttle mid-repair and leaves a medical engineer tumbling through orbit with a dwindling oxygen supply and no obvious way down. The long unbroken takes and the silence do all the work; the grief backstory is the one part that creaks.

Staff at an English hospital conduct their feuds, crushes and petty humiliations almost entirely away from patients, at speeds the editing keeps distorting. Sketch-show timing stretched to an hour, with speed-ramping and an unrepeatable cast, closer to a farce about desire than a workplace comedy.

A salesman with a borrowed vision, a reluctant hardware engineer and a young programmer reverse-engineer an IBM PC in early-eighties Texas and set about building something better. Starts as a Mad Men pastiche and grows into a great show about people who keep having to start over.

A masterless samurai turns up at a powerful clan's gate asking permission to commit ritual suicide in their courtyard, and the retainers receiving him have heard the request before. Kobayashi lays out his case against the samurai code so patiently that the last act arrives as a verdict rather than a twist.

Guns move through Hong Kong for a syndicate that stores its stock in a hospital basement, pursued by a hard-drinking inspector and an undercover officer he cannot read. Woo's action grammar at full stretch, and the hospital sequence is still the standard other shootouts get measured against.

Two brothers work a run of small West Texas bank branches to raise money against a foreclosure, while a Ranger weeks from retirement reads the pattern and waits. A heist film that is really about debt, land, and who gets to keep either.

A nameless county official arrives at the Qin court claiming to have killed the king's three deadliest assassins, and recounts each killing in turn. Ravishing to look at, and quietly making a case for the unified state that is worth arguing back at.

On his wedding day a marshal learns the man he sent to prison is arriving on the noon train, and spends the morning asking a town that owes him for help. Told close to real time, and far more interested in civic cowardice than in gunplay.

Two centuries before the Targaryens lose their dragons, a king names his daughter heir and the court spends years deciding whether to honour it. More chamber drama than its parent show, which suits a succession fought first in council rooms and marriages.

A London writer with a book deadline pieces together a night out she cannot remember, and keeps living messily and funnily while she does it. Coel writes consent as something almost everyone negotiates badly, and refuses the tidy recovery arc the subject usually gets.

In early-seventies Harlem a young woman carrying her first child works with her family to free her fiancé from a charge they all know is false. Jenkins films tenderness and injustice in the same register, which makes the warm scenes ache more than the cruel ones.

A Tokyo bureaucrat who has shuffled paper for thirty years is told he has months left, and goes looking for one thing he can finish. The structure snaps in half partway through, and the second half is where its argument about a life lands.

Through a snowstorm a young woman travels to meet her boyfriend's parents at their remote farmhouse, and time inside the house refuses to behave. Kaufman on loneliness and the stories people tell to make a life scan; obtuse by design, and not for everyone.

Two Irish hitmen are ordered to lie low in a preserved medieval city after a job goes wrong, one sightseeing happily and the other coming apart. The jokes are filthy and the guilt underneath them is real, a harder balance than it looks.

In 1960s Hong Kong a man and a woman renting rooms in the same building work out that their spouses are seeing each other, and begin meeting to rehearse how it started. Restraint as method: almost nothing happens, repeatedly, and the accumulation is devastating.

Twin siblings in Montreal are handed two letters by their late mother's notary and sent to a Middle Eastern country she never spoke about. The plotting is engineered to a fault, but the war sequences have a plainness that stays with you.

A triad plant inside the Hong Kong police and an undercover officer inside the triad each learn a mole exists, and are each told to find the other. Tighter and sadder than the American remake, and far more interested in what the double life costs.

In occupied France a squad of Jewish-American soldiers hunting Nazis and a cinema owner with her own plan converge on a film premiere in Paris. Tarantino's best writing of tension, in long multilingual conversations where everyone is lying and the table could go off at any moment.

A folk singer in 1961 Greenwich Village carries his guitar and someone else's cat around the city, sleeping on sofas and sabotaging every break he gets. The Coens on failure with no redemption arc attached, and the music is played straight and beautifully.

Sent to an Alaskan town to work a teenage girl's murder, a Los Angeles detective makes a mistake in the fog and then cannot sleep through the endless daylight. Nolan's most conventional film and his most attentive to one guilty conscience, with Williams cast against type and underplaying it.

In Oxford a chief inspector who drinks real ale, does the crossword and loathes his own superiors works college murders with a patient Geordie sergeant doing the legwork. Feature-length and slow by design, where the class texture of the city matters as much as the puzzle.

With crops failing on a dying Earth, a former pilot leaves his children to fly through a wormhole looking for somewhere else the species can live. The relativity sequences are extraordinary; the dialogue explaining them less so, and the emotional case is made very loudly.

An alien arrival is told from the ground up through strangers scattered across continents, among them a Long Island mother, a Japanese mission controller and a soldier posted to Afghanistan. Patient to the point of frustrating early on, though the scale it eventually reaches is unusual for television.

A flight attendant running cash for an arms dealer is squeezed by federal agents and decides to play both sides, with a bail bondsman who likes her as cover. Tarantino's most adult film: patient, middle-aged, and more interested in two people talking at dusk than in the score.

Swimmers start dying off a New England resort island, and a police chief who hates the water is left arguing with a mayor who wants the beaches open for the season. Withholding the creature began as a production accident and turned into the whole method.

A retired hitman is pulled back out by a gangster's son who steals his car and kills the dog his late wife left him. Bluntly efficient action, shot so the geography stays legible, plus a hotel-and-gold-coin underworld the sequels would over-explain.

Two palaeontologists and a mathematician are flown to an island park stocked with cloned dinosaurs and asked to sign off on it before opening. The effects hold up because they are rationed, and the film understands that waiting frightens more than showing.

A US marshal with an old-fashioned attitude to drawing his weapon is reassigned to the eastern Kentucky county he grew up in, where the criminals are people he knows. Elmore Leonard dialogue done properly, and Goggins turns a one-episode villain into the show's second lead.

Waking from a coma years after her wedding party was shot up, a former assassin starts working through the list of colleagues who did it, beginning in a suburban kitchen. Pure pastiche of kung fu, spaghetti western and anime, sequenced as escalating duels rather than a plot.

Osage families made wealthy by oil in 1920s Oklahoma begin dying, and a returning veteran marries into one while his cattleman uncle runs the county. Scorsese refuses the detective shape the material invites and tells it from inside the marriage instead; long, and deliberately airless.

Three separate stories share a cast: a man whose employer dictates every detail of his life, a policeman convinced his rescued wife is an impostor, and two cultists seeking a woman who can raise the dead. Lanthimos back in deadpan-cruel mode, funnier than it is profound.

A Joseon-era crown prince investigating his father's illness rides south and finds a plague turning the starving dead into something that hunts at night. The zombie mechanics are borrowed, but the class politics and the hanbok-and-torchlight staging make it its own thing.

Released from prison as the Wall comes down, an East German assassin goes looking for the Stasi handlers who framed her. Pop-scored, arch and very violent, with a lightness that sometimes fights the real history it is standing on.

A small-town detective comes to New York to trace a missing friend and finds his only lead is a call girl being stalked by someone she cannot see. Fonda plays her as a woman narrating her own therapy, which turns a procedural into a study of who gets believed.

A gossip reporter drifts through seven Roman nights of film stars, staged miracles and parties that outlast everyone in them, looking for a life with some weight to it. Fellini builds it as episodes rather than plot, and the accumulation is the point; it is long, and deliberately exhausting.

Twenty-four hours in a Paris banlieue after a riot, with three friends killing time and one of them carrying a policeman's lost revolver. Shot in luminous black and white, it is less interested in the violence than in the boredom preceding it, and has not dated at all.

An aspiring actress and a purist jazz pianist meet in a Los Angeles built for wanting things, and their careers start pulling apart almost as soon as the romance begins. The songs are slighter than the filmmaking around them, but the closing sequence justifies the whole enterprise.

A Sacramento teenager in her last year of Catholic school renames herself, picks fights with her mother and plots an escape to somewhere with culture. Gerwig gets the mother-daughter register exactly right: two people who cannot stop wounding each other and cannot stop talking either.

Sent into the Arabian desert during the First World War, a junior British officer turns out to be spectacularly and dangerously suited to it. Lean shoots landscape as psychology, and the second half is unusually honest about what the empire's promises to its allies were worth.

A teenage child actor and a woman in her mid-twenties with no plan circle each other across the San Fernando Valley of 1973, starting businesses and abandoning them. Anderson is after the texture of a place and a year rather than a story, and leaves the age gap uncomfortable on purpose.

Four sisters grow up in wartime Massachusetts, and one of them later tries to sell the story of it to a publisher who wants the ending changed. Gerwig cuts between childhood and adulthood so each scene comments on the other, turning a familiar book into an argument about authorship.

Raised on the Arsene Lupin novels, a Parisian thief uses disguise, misdirection and the city itself to avenge his father against the wealthy family that destroyed him. Omar Sy carries it on charm alone, and the capers work as light entertainment rather than plausible crime.

A London murder detective with a real gift for reading killers keeps breaking the rules that would make his cases stick, and his private life pays the bill. Elba is magnetic and the serial-killer plotting is lurid; his double act with a cheerfully amoral murderer is the reason to stay.

In a desert ruled by a warlord who hoards the water, a commander smuggles five women out in a war rig and a captured drifter is dragged along for it. Miller stages almost all of it practically, and the world-building happens in the corners rather than in dialogue.

Over one day in the San Fernando Valley a dying television producer, a self-help guru selling misogyny, a coke-addled former quiz champion and a lonely policeman all bend toward the same reckoning. Wildly overextended and completely sincere; Cruise's performance is the best thing he has done.

A retired profiler who thinks his way into killers' heads is pulled back to catch one murdering whole families, which means consulting the cannibal who nearly finished him. Mann's first Lecter film trades gore for cold blue design and synthesisers, and is far stranger than the remake.

Drunk and laid up with a broken leg, a Hollywood screenwriter drafts Citizen Kane while remembering the studio politics and the newspaper baron who gave him his material. Fincher reproduces the look and sound of 1940s Hollywood precisely; you do need to care about the argument over credit.

A London detective returns to the murder squad after years away, working a case that resembles one she never closed and blacking out for stretches she cannot account for. The premise is stronger than the plotting, which piles on subplots and asks you to forgive some very large coincidences.

In a small Pennsylvania town where she has known everyone for decades, a detective investigates the killing of a young mother while a missing-girl case she never solved hangs over her. Winslet plays exhaustion rather than grit, and the town's texture matters more than the whodunnit.

A theatre director and the actress who has been his lead try to separate amicably, then hire lawyers and watch the process turn their lives into evidence. Baumbach is scrupulously even-handed, and sharpest on how the legal machinery manufactures cruelty neither of them intended.

The long-serving mayor of Marseille plans to hand the city to his protege and ends up in a street fight for it instead, with the docks, the drug trade and the local press all in play. Depardieu is watchable; the writing is broad, and it plays as soap rather than statecraft.

Two provincial detectives and a methodical colleague sent from Seoul hunt a serial killer in 1980s rural Korea with almost no forensic resources and a police culture that prefers confessions. Bong holds slapstick and dread in the same scene without either cancelling the other; the frustration is the real subject.

During Prohibition, an Irish mob boss's right-hand man plays both sides of a gang war fought over a bookmaker nobody much wants to protect. The Coens write it in a hard-boiled dialect so dense it takes a reel to tune into, and it rewards both the effort and a second viewing.

A Korean immigrant family move to rural Arkansas so the father can farm, and the grandmother who follows them over unsettles the household in ways nobody planned for. Chung keeps the register small and unsentimental, letting the marriage strain quietly instead of building it into a set piece.

In a Washington where murders are predicted and stopped before they happen, the officer running the unit is named by the system as a future killer and goes on the run. Spielberg's interface design and grimy future have aged well; the last stretch explains itself rather more than it needs to.

The memories of a dying man arrive without chronology or explanation: a burning barn, a mother at a printing press, wartime newsreel, his own childhood folded into his son's. It asks to be watched rather than followed, and works far better once you stop trying to reconstruct a story.

Five young offenders doing community service on an Essex estate are caught in a freak storm and come out with powers that mostly embarrass them. The first two series are sharp, filthy and genuinely inventive about what ordinary people would do with a gift like this; the later cast changes hurt it.

A boy growing up poor, black and quiet in Miami is shown at three ages, from bullied child to cornered teenager to hardened man, working out who he is permitted to be. Jenkins shoots close and in saturated colour, and the silences carry far more than the dialogue does.

On a New England island in 1965 a scout and a girl with a suitcase of stolen library books run away together, and the search party of adults exposes its own unhappiness. Anderson's most emotionally direct film, because the symmetry and dollhouse framing read as the children's view of things.

Middle-class parents at a London primary school compete, panic and quietly sabotage each other over childcare, birthday parties and the school run. Written with real venom and almost no warmth, it is the funniest British sitcom about class in years, and Diane Morgan's slumped fatalism steals it.

A Sydney man does the school run, manages his daughter, dates, sits with his dying brother, and in between all of it beats and kills people for money. Scott Ryan plays it completely flat, which makes the violence land hard and the half-hour format feel like a small discovery.

Two girls from a poor Naples neighbourhood in the 1950s build a friendship out of love and competition in equal measure, and the series follows them from childhood towards middle age. Cast with non-professionals and played in Neapolitan dialect, it takes Ferrante's ambivalence seriously rather than softening it.

A middle-aged structural engineer worn down by his family and his office and a young woman surviving debt and violence fall into a careful, unlikely alliance. Slow, sad and entirely unromantic about the age gap; the closing episodes are among the most moving Korean television has produced.

Two sisters move to a country house while their mother lies in a nearby hospital, and discover the woods next door are full of large, sleepy spirits. Almost nothing happens by design — the tension is a child's worry about a parent, handled with extraordinary patience.

DEA agents in Bogotá chase the Medellín cartel while its founder builds a business that outgrows the state trying to stop it. The archive footage and hindsight-heavy narration do a lot of the lifting, but Moura's performance keeps it from playing as a slideshow.

A veteran news anchor announces his own on-air suicide, and his network, smelling ratings, gives him a nightly pulpit instead of a doctor. Chayefsky's satire has been overtaken by reality so completely that it now plays closer to reportage than to comedy.

After the town built around a single plant is wiped off the map, a widow in her sixties loads a van and joins the seasonal-work circuit across the American West. Real nomads play themselves alongside McDormand, and the film is far better at listening than at plotting.

Siblings running a failing horse ranch that supplies Hollywood spot something living in the clouds above their land, and decide the way out is to film it. Peele's most formally ambitious film: a Western about the price of spectacle, with a monster nobody has built before.

Two Sligo teenagers keep finding each other — at school, at Trinity, through each other's worst years — without ever managing to say the plain thing. Half-hour episodes and long silences; the adaptation trusts its actors' faces to carry what the novel did in free indirect prose.

An advertising man is mistaken for a spy who does not exist, and spends the next two thousand miles running from people who refuse to accept the correction. The template for every chase picture since, and lighter on its feet than any of the descendants.

The daughter of a convicted Nazi is recruited by American intelligence to marry her way into a circle of German exiles in Rio. A romance in which the man keeps pimping the woman he loves — the cruellest film Hitchcock made, and the most adult.

A man is locked in a furnished room for fifteen years without explanation, then released with a phone, a wad of cash and a deadline to find out who did it. The corridor fight gets the attention, but the film's real subject is how badly revenge scales.

Jewish gangsters rise out of the Lower East Side through Prohibition, and one of them comes back decades later to find the past rearranged around him. Elegiac and morally queasy in equal measure; the long cut drifts badly in places and is still the only version worth watching.

A fading television cowboy and his stunt double drift through Los Angeles in 1969, taking meetings and running errands while a new Hollywood arrives without them. Tarantino's hangout movie — plot-light, texture-rich, and built entirely around an ending you can feel coming for two hours.

Land the railroad needs passes to a widow arriving from New Orleans, and three men with unrelated reasons converge on her farm. Leone slows everything to a crawl so that a hat brim or a harmonica note carries the weight a speech normally would.

A convict fakes insanity to serve his sentence somewhere softer, and finds the psychiatric ward run by a nurse whose authority is total and never raised above a murmur. A film about institutions rather than illness — its view of psychiatric medicine has aged badly, its view of power has not.

Watching a woman with her exact face step in front of a train, a street hustler steals the dead woman's identity and lands inside a network of monitored clones. Maslany plays a dozen roles well enough that you stop noticing the trick; the conspiracy plotting gets away from the show long before she does.

A Second World War combat nurse touches a standing stone in the Highlands and wakes in 1743, married off for protection to a Jacobite clansman. It takes romance seriously as a genre rather than smuggling it in, and is franker about sex and its consequences than most prestige drama manages.

Staged on the exact line between Germany and Austria, a body forces a by-the-book German detective into partnership with a burnt-out Austrian who barely observes procedure. Cold, slow and openly indebted to The Bridge, though Ofczarek's shambling wreck of a policeman is entirely its own creation.

On their first night in a Manhattan brownstone, a divorced woman and her diabetic daughter seal themselves into the hidden room the burglars downstairs need to reach. Fincher treating a single-location thriller as an exercise in geometry: efficient, cold, and minor by his standards.

In Spain in 1944, the stepdaughter of a Francoist officer hunting rebels in the hills is told by a faun that she is a lost princess with three tasks to complete. The fairy tale and the war are shot with the same matter-of-fact cruelty, which is exactly the point.

A bullied teenager starts getting messages from her dead father, who turns out to have been uploaded — a scanned mind running on servers owned by the company he worked for. Rigorous science fiction about digital immortality, and rare in animation for following its premise all the way down.

Therapists can enter their patients' dreams using a new device, and when one is stolen the researcher who moonlights inside it must chase a spreading delusion through other people's heads. Kon does in a single cut what later films needed a scene of explanation to set up.

A relentlessly optimistic deputy director in a small Indiana town's parks department sets out to turn a derelict pit into a park, and keeps going for seven years. It starts as a thin Office clone and becomes the warmest ensemble comedy American television has produced.

Two childhood friends separated when one family leaves Seoul reconnect online as adults, then meet in New York twenty-four years later, by which time one of them is married. Almost nothing is said outright; it is a film about the life not taken that never once sentimentalises it.

After a suicidal attack on a German position collapses, three French soldiers are picked at random for court martial so that the generals who ordered it stay covered. Kubrick lets the tracking shots through the trenches make the argument, and the courtroom half is as cold as anything he filmed.

Two flatmates in Croydon — a joyless loan-company drone and his sponging former bandmate — narrate their own thoughts while their lives fail to improve for nine series. The point-of-view camera and the inner monologue make every social humiliation inescapable; the cringe sits closer to horror than comedy.

A pop idol leaves her group for acting, takes a role that requires her to be degraded on camera, and picks up a stalker who prefers the version of her that used to sing. Kon's first feature, and still the sharpest thing anyone has made about a persona eating its owner.

Struck mute mid-performance, an actress is sent to a coastal house with a nurse who talks enough for both of them, until the line between the two women stops holding. Bergman takes his own film apart on screen; short, difficult, and the source of a great deal of the visual vocabulary art film has used since.

A celebrated London couturier in the 1950s installs a young waitress as his muse, and she declines to be arranged like one of his dresses. It is a comedy once you notice it is one — about a marriage negotiated through control, illness and extremely good tailoring.

Back in Cornwall from the American war, a soldier finds his father dead, the family mine failing and his fiancée engaged to his cousin. Handsome Sunday-night drama that is considerably more interested in copper prices and rural poverty than its shirtless reputation suggests.

A Victorian surgeon revives a drowned woman with an infant's brain, and she teaches herself the world at speed — appetite first, manners a long way behind. Lanthimos at his most ornate; the fish-eye grotesquerie is a lot to sit with, and Stone's physical performance earns every frame of it.

Dropped into a Central American jungle on what they are told is a rescue job, a special-forces team works out that something is hunting them one at a time. It shifts quietly from a muscle-bound action picture into survival horror about being outclassed, and the switch still lands.

A young prince, cursed by a dying boar god, rides west into a war between an iron-working town and the forest spirits whose trees it is felling. Miyazaki refuses to hand either side the moral high ground, and the film is angrier and bloodier than its family-animation reputation suggests.

On the run with forty thousand stolen dollars, a secretary stops for the night at a roadside motel run by a shy young man and his mother. Hitchcock builds the whole thing as a trap for the audience's sympathies, and the cheap television-crew photography only makes it nastier.

Two hitmen, a boxer who fails to take a dive and a mob wife's night out interlock across a Los Angeles where the talk matters more than the violence. The shuffled chronology gets the credit, but it is the patience of the dialogue scenes that has aged best.

A lonely novelty-toy salesman with a rage problem buys pudding for the air miles, gets tangled in a phone-sex scam, and falls for a woman who sees past the flinching. Anderson turns Sandler's man-child persona inside out and scores the romance like an anxiety attack.

In the Bronx, a middleweight boxer fights his way towards the title while wrecking his marriage and his brother with the same jealous fury. Scorsese shoots the bouts as hallucination and the domestic scenes as documentary, which turns out to be the whole argument.

An archaeologist is hired to find the Ark of the Covenant before Hitler's agents do, which means Nepal, Cairo and a great many snakes. A serial-adventure pastiche made with more craft than almost anything it inspired, and the pacing is still the benchmark.

Two androids raise a handful of human children on a barren planet after Earth is lost to a religious war, until survivors of the losing faith arrive and wreck the experiment. Swings between extraordinary imagery and incoherence; Amanda Collin holds it together, and it was cancelled before the story lands.

An Egyptian-American in New Jersey tries to be a good Muslim and a good son, and keeps failing at both in ways the show refuses to excuse. Funnier about faith than almost anything else on television, and increasingly unwilling to make its lead likeable.

Dividing his domain between three sons, an ageing warlord discovers far too late what he has spent his life teaching them. Kurosawa recasts Lear in Sengoku Japan and stages the battles in near-silence; the colour and scale are overwhelming and deliberately hollow.

A woodcutter, a bandit, a samurai's wife and the dead samurai himself each give an incompatible account of a killing in a forest grove. The structure has been borrowed so often that its force is easy to underrate; watch how sunlight and rain make the truth feel physically out of reach.

Laid up with a broken leg, a press photographer spends the heatwave watching his neighbours across the courtyard and becomes convinced one of them has murdered his wife. Built entirely from one man's sightline, it makes the audience complicit in the snooping well before it makes them anxious about it.

After a jewellery heist goes wrong offscreen, the surviving thieves regroup in an empty warehouse to work out which of them informed. Tarantino's debut runs on suspicion and cheap talk, and the notorious torture scene still overshadows how tightly the rest is built.

A nihilistic genius drags his anxious grandson through infinite universes, and the family he keeps abandoning gets pulled along behind. The high-concept science fiction is inventive enough to carry the misanthropy, but the show is at its sharpest when it stops to notice the damage.

Detectives in Whitechapel police the East End in the years just after the Ripper killings, in a district that has become a tourist attraction for its own horror. Better on Victorian forensics and class than on its case-of-the-week plotting, and Macfadyen plays exhaustion beautifully.

In a 1986 Cotswolds carved up by commercial television, a Tory minister and a chat-show host conduct a feud through the local franchise, their marriages and everyone else's. A Jilly Cooper adaptation that commits fully to the silliness and the sex, and is far sharper on class than it needs to be.

A live-in maid to a middle-class family in early-1970s Mexico City keeps the household running through the year that breaks it, and the country, apart. Cuarón films his own childhood in wide monochrome and points the camera at the servant rather than the family; the restraint is the argument.

Two Roman soldiers, one rigidly dutiful and one all appetite, keep colliding with the end of the Republic and the men bringing it down. The politics are told from the gutter as much as the Senate, and the show cares more about patronage and household religion than about battles.

Minutes after strangling a classmate for the thrill of it, two students host a drinks party in the flat where the body is hidden, with the dead man's family among the guests. The stitched long takes are the famous gimmick; the real tension is watching two arrogant young men keep talking.

A woman in Berlin has twenty minutes to find a hundred thousand marks and save her boyfriend, and the film runs those twenty minutes three times over. A techno-scored formal experiment about how small contingencies fan out; propulsive, brief, and slighter than its reputation.

The worst student and most prolific club founder at a private prep school befriends a depressed steel magnate, then competes with him for a widowed teacher. Anderson's first fully formed film and still his cruellest, with Murray's deadpan misery as the counterweight to the whimsy.

When his estranged daughter goes missing, a feckless south-London chancer with no standing in her life starts looking for her anyway. Lennie James wrote it as well as starring, and it is unusually good on the estate and the drinkers who close ranks around him.

A ranger captain leads a squad across Normandy to pull one paratrooper out of the line because his three brothers are already dead. The opening landing changed how war is filmed; what follows is a more conventional and more sentimental picture than that reputation implies.

Two sisters join the IRA in 1970s Belfast, and decades later the question of who ordered a widowed mother of ten taken from her flat refuses to stay buried. Adapted from Keefe's book with a real willingness to sit inside the conviction of its young volunteers before the reckoning arrives.

A Cuban refugee lands in Miami in 1980 with nothing and takes the cocaine trade by being more willing than anyone around him. Excessive on purpose and an hour too long, but De Palma's vulgarity is doing real work on the decade that produced it.

Survivors of a wrecked freighter are scattered across a planet whose ecology is intricate, beautiful and entirely indifferent to them. The creature design carries the storytelling, with almost no exposition, and the invented biology is worked out more rigorously than most live-action science fiction manages.

A German industrialist profits from Jewish labour in occupied Kraków, then spends everything he has made keeping his workers off the transports. Spielberg at his most disciplined, and Fiennes makes the camp commandant's offhand cruelty the hardest thing in it to sit through.

Working a series of murders staged around the deadly sins, a detective days from retirement breaks in the impatient younger man taking his desk. Fincher's rain and rot do most of the work, and the film is unusually serious about what the job costs the men doing it.

Four New Yorkers with no redeeming ambitions turn queueing, parking and second dates into nine seasons of escalating social crime. The plotting is the real achievement, three strands converging on one payoff week after week, along with the refusal to let anybody learn anything.

In eight cities at once, strangers find they can share each other's senses, skills and memories, which makes them useful to one another and hunted by an organisation. Wildly uneven and sincerely utopian; the action matters less than the argument that empathy is a physical fact.

A farming village bled every harvest by bandits hires seven masterless swordsmen with rice it can barely spare. The template for every assembled-team film since, though the original is really about class, and the farmers' fear of their own protectors never quite lifts.

A New York executive keeps his flat immaculate and his compulsions hidden, until his chaotic sister turns up with nowhere else to stay and no sense of boundaries. McQueen shoots addiction as cold architecture, all long unbroken takes and grey glass, and refuses to hand anyone a redemption arc.

Murders wash up on a remote Scottish archipelago where everyone knows everyone, and the detective investigating them grew up among the suspects. The landscape does half the work, bleak and wind-scoured, and the pacing is patient in a way that rewards anyone who likes their crime drama unhurried.

A makeshift Tokyo family scrape by on petty theft and pooled benefits, and take in a neglected girl they find shivering on a balcony. Kore-eda builds an hour of warmth before quietly asking what actually makes a family, and the answer is less comforting than the first act suggests.

Thirty years apart, a modern profiler and a detective working the same unsolved cases start trading information over a battered walkie-talkie that should not work at all. The time-travel conceit is really a delivery system for grief and institutional rot, and the cold cases are drawn from real Korean crimes.

Five engineers turn a lossless compression algorithm into a startup and discover that the hard part is never the code. Judge's satire is precise enough that people in the industry watched it as documentary, and it stays funny by letting its characters fail on their own terms.

Returning to 1930s Mississippi, twin brothers open a juke joint whose music on the first night draws something far older than the Klan to the door. Coogler fuses Delta blues, Jim Crow history and vampire horror without letting any one of the three swallow the other two.

A Bristol sixth-form crowd chase parties, sex and drugs while the adults around them fail in ways the show takes seriously. Each pair of series replaces the entire cast, which keeps the energy but means the quality swings hard: the first two generations hold up, the later ones much less so.

Humanity's survivors circle a frozen earth aboard a thousand-carriage train where your carriage is your class, and a tail-section detective is dragged forward to solve a murder. The series has more room than the film for the politics of the engine, but trades Bong's savage compression for procedural filler.

A psychologist travels to a station orbiting a sentient ocean planet, where the crew are being visited by physical copies of people from their pasts. Tarkovsky turns science fiction inward until it is about guilt and memory rather than contact, at a pace that asks real patience and repays it.

Hearing loss arrives almost overnight for the drummer of a two-person noise band, who is packed off to a sober house for deaf addicts he has no intention of joining. The sound design puts you inside the loss, and the film is about accepting a life rather than repairing one.

A sulky ten-year-old's parents are turned into pigs at an abandoned theme park, and she has to take work in a bathhouse for spirits to win them back. Miyazaki lets the world stay strange and unexplained, and the quiet stretches, like a train ride over flooded water, are what linger.

Hundreds of desperate debtors accept an invitation to compete in childhood playground games for a vast cash prize, on terms they only grasp after the first round. The first season's argument about debt and class is sharp; the two that follow stretch the premise further than it comfortably goes.

Twenty years after a flu collapses civilisation, a travelling troupe performs Shakespeare around the Great Lakes while the world before keeps intruding on the people who remember it. Adapted from Mandel's novel with unusual generosity, it is a post-apocalypse about art and continuity rather than scarcity and violence.

Kids in a 1980s Indiana town lose a friend to something living underneath their world, and a girl with a shaved head and unexplained powers turns up in his place. The Spielberg and King borrowings are worn openly; what makes it work is the children, cast and written better than the plot deserves.

A tennis player makes idle conversation with a charming stranger who proposes they swap murders, and works out too late that only one of them was joking. Walker's performance is the engine, flirtatious and unmoored, decades ahead of the rest of the film in what it dares to imply.

Broke and dodging repo men, a screenwriter takes shelter in the decaying mansion of a silent-film star who has spent twenty years waiting for her comeback. Wilder got Hollywood to fund a film about its own cruelty to the people it discards, and the industry's discomfort is part of the pleasure.

A theatre director wins a large grant and spends decades building a full-scale replica of New York inside a warehouse, casting actors to play everyone in his life. Kaufman's densest and saddest film, about mortality and self-absorption; it will either overwhelm you or exhaust you, and both responses are defensible.

In a small American town built above a subterranean physics experiment, ordinary residents meet machines and anomalies that rearrange their lives in small, irreversible ways. Loosely linked episodes drawn from Simon Stalenhag's paintings, melancholy rather than thrilling, and lovely to look at if you can accept the slowness.

An insomniac Vietnam veteran drives nights through a New York he finds filthy, and talks himself steadily towards a violent act he can call righteous. Scorsese and Schrader lock the perspective inside a man who is wrong about almost everything, which is exactly why it still unsettles.

Recruited into a shadow operation and briefed mostly in fragments, an unnamed agent finds himself fighting a war with objects and people whose entropy runs backwards. The set pieces are unlike anything else and the sound mix buries the exposition; take it as a puzzle box rather than for feeling.

A reprogrammed killing machine is sent back to protect the boy it was once built to kill, while a shape-shifting newer model hunts them and his mother plans to stop the war outright. Cameron's action grammar is still clear as glass, and Hamilton gives the spectacle something to be about.

A century after nuclear war, a dying space station drops a hundred juvenile prisoners onto a possibly survivable earth to find out whether it is. It starts as teen survival drama and hardens into something considerably bleaker about leadership and atrocity, though the middle seasons sprawl badly.

Ignored at home and punished at school, a Paris schoolboy drifts into truancy and petty theft that every adult around him reads as proof of a bad character. Truffaut's first feature, made from his own childhood, and its closing shot is one of the reasons the New Wave mattered.

A CIA officer is pulled out of six years of deep cover and ordered back to London station, where the woman he left behind reappears and his legend starts to fray. An adaptation of the French series Le Bureau that keeps the tradecraft procedural and the emotions suppressed.

In the outlaw's last months, a hero-worshipping young hanger-on attaches himself to the gang and slowly curdles into something else. Dominik and Deakins make a western that moves like an elegy, and since the title gives away the plot, the tension is entirely psychological.

A lifelong friendship on a small Irish island ends by unilateral declaration in 1923: one man simply stops speaking to the other and will not say why. McDonagh plays a civil war in miniature for laughs that keep catching in the throat, and Condon has the film's clearest eye.

A serial killer begins murdering Gotham officials and leaving riddles for a Batman who is two years into the job and still closer to a stalker than a symbol. Reeves shoots it as a rain-soaked detective picture; it is long, and the pleasure is in the investigation rather than the fights.

The FLN's urban campaign against French colonial rule in Algiers, and the paratroop colonel brought in to break it by whatever method is available. Pontecorvo shoots it like newsreel and lets neither side off, which is why armies it indicts have screened it as a training film.

A fine-dining chef inherits his late brother's chaotic Chicago sandwich shop, along with its debts and a staff who resent him on sight. The kitchen noise and overlapping panic are exact, and the show is better on grief and family obligation than on food; the bottle episodes are where it peaks.

Mistaken for a millionaire who shares his name, a Los Angeles slacker is pulled into a kidnapping plot he is in every way unequipped to follow. The Coens' shaggiest film, built out of digressions and a bowling alley, where the plot's incoherence is the actual joke.

British prisoners of war in a Japanese camp in Burma are ordered to build a railway bridge, and their colonel decides to build a good one. Lean stages the spectacle beautifully, but the real subject is how easily pride rebrands itself as duty.

Two Copenhagen detectives work a killing where a small figure made of chestnuts has been left at the scene, and the trail reaches back to a politician's missing daughter. Handsome, grim Nordic procedural that leans harder on plot mechanics than on the people carrying them.

A San Francisco surveillance expert records a couple talking in a crowded square and begins to suspect his tape will get them killed. Hackman plays paranoia as a professional deformation, a man who guards his own privacy so fiercely there is nothing left inside it.

Born elderly in New Orleans and ageing backwards, a man drifts through the twentieth century, forever out of step with the woman he loves. Fincher's most sentimental film is technically astonishing and emotionally becalmed; the conceit does more work than the romance resting on it.

Gotham's masked vigilante, its crusading district attorney and a weary lieutenant close in on organised crime, until an anarchist in face paint turns their alliance into an experiment. Ledger is why it endures, but the escalating structure of moral traps is what makes it hold.

Eight years into retirement, a broken Wayne returns to a Gotham squeezed by a masked mercenary preaching revolution and a burglar running her own angles. Bigger and more ponderous than its predecessor, with genuine weight in the prison sequences and a plot that creaks under its scale.

At an isolated orphanage during the Spanish Civil War, a new boy finds an unexploded bomb in the courtyard and a drowned child who will not stay quiet. Del Toro's ghost story is really about the adults; the war seeps in long before anything supernatural does.

Two cousins compete for the attention of an ailing Queen Anne while the war with France drags on and the court watches for weakness. Lanthimos plays period drama as a cruel comedy of dependency, and Colman finds the frightened, gouty woman under the crown.

A six-year-old and her young mother scrape by in a violet-painted motel in the shadow of Disney World, watched over by a patient manager. Baker shoots childhood summer as pure joy while letting the precariousness sit in the frame, and never lectures.

Old New York money and brash new railway money face off across a Manhattan street in the 1880s, with a newly orphaned niece caught between the houses. Fellowes doing Downton in America: plush, slow, and best when the Black middle-class Brooklyn strand takes the floor.

A disgraced financial journalist is hired to solve a forty-year-old disappearance on an industrialist's private island, and gains an unlikely partner in a hacker with a photographic memory. Rapace makes Salander a genuinely unsettling presence; the mystery around her is sturdy, unhurried, cold-blooded pulp.

The ageing head of a New York crime family is shot, and his youngest son, the decorated war hero who wanted no part of the business, steps into the vacuum. Coppola films organised crime as domestic ritual, which is why the violence lands so quietly.

A Sicilian immigrant's rise in old New York runs alongside his son's colder, lonelier expansion into Havana and Nevada half a century later. The cross-cutting is the argument: what the father built by hand, the son can only defend by subtraction.

Detectives chase the bullion from the 1983 Brink's-Mat robbery as it moves through smelters, solicitors and Spanish property deals, reshaping London on the way. Less a heist drama than a study of laundering, with Bonneville's dogged copper anchoring a story about money's afterlife.

Three gunmen circle a cache of Confederate gold across a Civil War landscape, each holding a piece of the answer and none able to trust the others. Leone stretches time until a glance becomes an event, and Morricone's score does half the directing.

A legendary concierge at a mountain-top hotel between the wars is left a priceless painting by a wealthy guest, then framed for her murder. Anderson's most controlled confection, with a real melancholy about vanished European civility running underneath all the pink.

A pickpocket is planted as maid to a Japanese heiress on a remote estate in colonial Korea, part of a conman's plan to marry and commit her. Park tells it three times over, each pass rewriting who was using whom; sumptuous, funny and properly erotic.

In a theocratic America that has stripped women of names, work and property, the few who remain fertile are assigned to powerful households as state-sanctioned breeding stock. The first season is close to unbearable in the right way; later ones stretch thinner while Moss keeps finding registers.

Four suburban sixth-formers fail at girls, parties and basic dignity with a commitment bordering on the heroic. It stays funny because the boys are never allowed to be cool or secretly wise; the humiliation is the point, and it is observed with real accuracy.
