A sacked tobacco scientist decides to break his confidentiality agreement on television, and the producer who courted him discovers his own network would rather not air it. Mann shoots corporate cowardice like a thriller, and Crowe plays a difficult, frightened man rather than a hero.

A truck driver turned mob enforcer in post-war Pennsylvania rises through the unions and into the orbit of a missing labour leader. Three and a half hours that earn their length in the final forty minutes, a gangster epic about being outlived by your own choices.

Two antisocial technicians and the manager who knows nothing about computers run the support department from a basement beneath an absurd corporation. Broad, joke-dense studio sitcom in the old British mould, carried by Ayoade's delivery and a refusal to pretend office life makes sense.

An aspiring stand-up with no act and total conviction stalks a late-night host, then decides to take his shot by other means. Scorsese and De Niro made the least flattering film about fame ever attempted, and it has only grown more accurate since.

A cocaine-addicted surgeon runs the operating theatre of a struggling New York hospital in 1900, where new procedures are invented and patients die teaching them. Soderbergh shot and cut every episode himself; the electronic score and cold light make medical history feel genuinely dangerous.

Born Saxon and raised Dane, a displaced nobleman fights for Alfred's idea of a united England while trying to win back his family's stolen fortress. Sturdy, brisk historical action that takes its politics more seriously than its battles and knows how good its loyalty problem is.

In a society where single adults have forty-five days to find a partner or be turned into an animal, a newly abandoned man checks into the hotel where matching happens. Lanthimos's deadpan absurdism cuts hardest in the second half, when escape proves just as rule-bound.

Philip Marlowe drives a friend to Tijuana, comes home to a murder charge, and shuffles through a 1970s Los Angeles with no use for his code. Altman's mumbling, cat-feeding revision of the private eye is the best joke anyone has played on the genre.

Two decades after the Axis won, occupied America is split between a Nazi east and a Japanese west, and newsreels showing a different outcome begin circulating. Superb production design and a terrific Rufus Sewell, though the plotting loses its grip as the mystery keeps expanding.

Left for dead on Mars, an astronaut has to grow food, make water and signal home using the equipment a scrubbed mission abandoned. Scott's most cheerful film in years is a procedural about competence, where the tension comes from arithmetic rather than menace.

A drifting, drink-ruined navy veteran attaches himself to the charismatic founder of a new philosophical movement in post-war America. Anderson has no interest in exposing the cult; the film is about the need that makes a man want to be owned, and Phoenix is extraordinary.

A low-level FBI agent manning a phone in the White House basement that is never supposed to ring picks it up one night and is pulled into a conspiracy running up through the administration. Efficient, unpretentious Netflix thriller that moves fast enough that you rarely notice how thin the plotting is.

The staff of a Slough paper merchant are followed by a documentary crew while their branch manager performs relentlessly for the camera and nobody stops him. Short, precisely engineered and genuinely uncomfortable; almost every workplace comedy since has been looser and kinder by comparison.

Cameras follow the sales staff of a Pennsylvania paper company through birthday parties, fire drills and a regional manager who desperately wants to be everyone's friend. It takes a season to shed the British original's meanness and find its own warmth, then sustains that for years.

A Missouri farmer whose family is killed by Union irregulars rides west with a bounty on his head, collecting a ragged group of strays he never asked for. Eastwood's warmest western: the revenge plot keeps giving way to an accidental, often funny community.

Repressed, controlling and still living with her mother, a Viennese conservatoire professor begins a punishing affair with a confident young student. Huppert plays it without a flicker of appeal for sympathy, and Haneke films the cruelty at a clinical distance that makes it harder, not easier, to watch.

In the Australian outback of the 1880s, a captured bushranger is offered his younger brother's life in exchange for hunting down and killing his older one. Nick Cave's script strips the western back to heat, flies and consequence; beautiful and brutal in roughly equal measure.

A police squad enters a Jakarta tower block owned by a drug lord and finds every floor between them and the street filled with men holding machetes. Close to a pure action machine: the silat choreography is exceptional and the plot exists mainly to keep the corridors coming.

Six years after a rain-borne virus empties Scandinavia, a Danish brother and sister leave the bunker that kept them alive and join a group of survivors crossing the ruins. Strong premise, patchy follow-through; the emptied Denmark is atmospheric but the group's squabbling eats episodes that should be moving.

A young CIA lawyer barely out of training opens a letter from an imprisoned former asset threatening to expose the agency, and is sent to handle her alone. Centineo plays out of his depth well, and it works better as a comedy of bureaucratic panic than as a spy thriller.

Nights on urgent response in Liverpool with a demoted, unravelling police constable whose coping arrangements crossed into the criminal some time ago. Written by a former officer and anchored by a superb Freeman performance; grim, but never merely miserable, and the humour is real.

Three grown child prodigies move back into the family brownstone when their estranged father announces he is dying, which he is not. Anderson's symmetry and deadpan fully arrive here, but the film holds up because the melancholy underneath is played entirely straight.

A Tehran couple staging Death of a Salesman move into a new flat, where an intrusion by a stranger sends the husband on a private hunt for the man responsible. Farhadi's usual method: no villain anywhere, just people whose reasonable choices close around each other.

In a Los Angeles precinct, a bullish detective's strike team closes the cases nobody else can while quietly running the neighbourhood as a protection racket. Seven seasons of steadily tightening consequence, and one of very few crime shows that follows its premise all the way to the end it deserves.

Hired to mind an empty Colorado hotel through the winter, a blocked writer moves his wife and young son in, and the boy begins seeing things. Kubrick's geometry does the frightening work, corridors that cannot exist and a camera gliding just behind a child, rather than anything he actually shows you.

A trainee FBI agent is sent to interview an imprisoned cannibal psychiatrist in the hope he will help her identify a killer who is still working. The interview scenes are the film; Demme's straight-to-camera close-ups put you inside the cell rather than beside it.

Life in an American town built around a nuclear plant, centred on the family of its least competent safety inspector. The golden run in the mid-nineties is still the densest joke-writing television has managed, and the show has been living off that goodwill for decades since.

A fading television fitness star takes a black-market drug that produces a younger duplicate of her, on the strict condition that the two swap weeks. The body horror is extravagant and the satire is hammered rather than aimed, which is either the flaw or the whole point.

At an Antarctic research station, an American crew takes in a dog fleeing a destroyed Norwegian camp and learns what came with it: something that perfectly imitates whatever it kills. Bottin's effects still hold, but the paranoia does the real work, because nobody in the room can be cleared.

A broke pulp novelist arrives in occupied Vienna to take a job from an old friend and is told the friend was buried that morning. Tilted frames, a zither and endless rubble; the cynicism runs bone-deep and the final shot is as good as endings get.

Seven adopted children with powers, raised as a superhero team by a cold billionaire, reassemble as badly damaged adults when he dies. The dysfunctional-family comedy is the good part; the time-travel plotting grows more tangled every season and the finale divided most of the people still watching.

A Manhattan therapist's comfortable life comes apart when a violent death in her son's school circle puts her husband at the centre of a murder investigation. Kidman and Grant are excellent company, and the six episodes are handsome and hollow, more interested in coats than in clues.

Chicago under Prohibition, where a Treasury agent assembles a small incorruptible team to go after Capone because every other official in the city is bought. De Palma stages it as opera, Morricone scores it as one, and Connery gives the whole thing its spine.

A detective recalled from Oslo joins a Reykjavik investigator on a run of killings whose thread leads back to a boys' reform home. Competent rather than distinctive as Nordic procedurals go, carried by its two leads and the institutional-abuse story running underneath.

Each season checks a new set of wealthy guests into a different branch of a luxury resort chain and waits for their manners to fail. Mike White writes class comedy with a body in it: patient, cruel, and consistently better on the guests than on the staff.

Strange accidents and small cruelties accumulate in a north German village in the year before the First World War, and the schoolteacher starts to suspect the children. Shot in austere black and white, and pointedly refusing the explanation it spends two hours inviting you to demand.

A mutant monster-hunter for hire, a sorceress who remade herself through magic and a princess with a dangerous bloodline circle each other across a continent at war. The first season's scrambled timelines are worth persevering with; the later ones look expensive and drift ever further from the books.

Worthless shares sold hard out of a Long Island boiler room make a young broker rich enough to spend at a rate that becomes the film's real subject. Three hours of sustained mania, and the argument over whether Scorsese is indicting or enjoying it is the most interesting thing about it.

The first American pope turns out to be a reactionary who refuses to be photographed and treats the Vatican bureaucracy as an enemy to be broken. Sorrentino strings astonishing images on sly comedy; slow, strange, and nothing like the prestige-drama formula the premise suggests.

A Chicago safecracker with a precise plan for the ordinary life he wants takes one last job from the outfit and learns what that partnership actually costs. Mann's first feature already has the lot: Tangerine Dream, wet streets at night, and men explaining their professionalism at length.

Impossible shifts on an NHS obstetrics and gynaecology ward, seen through a junior doctor whose life outside the hospital is quietly collapsing. Adapted from Adam Kay's diaries and far darker than the comedy billing suggests, with the jokes there mainly to soften the blow.

A grieving mother rents three derelict billboards to shame the local police chief over her daughter's unsolved murder, and the whole town turns on her. McDonagh writes wonderfully cruel dialogue, but the film asks you to forgive a racist deputy rather faster than it has earned.

Inside a British prison, a teacher serving four years for a death he caused meets an officer being blackmailed through his own son. Each series tells a self-contained story, the second moving to a women's wing, and the writing refuses the usual prison-drama theatrics for something closer to documentary.

In Depression-era Alabama, a widowed lawyer defends a Black man accused of raping a white woman while his two children spend the summer daring each other towards the shuttered house next door. Peck is the monument, but the film belongs to the children's-eye view of adult cowardice.

An elderly couple travel from the provinces to visit their grown children in Tokyo, who are too busy and too irritated to want them. Ozu keeps the camera low and still while quietly indicting a whole generation, and the restraint is exactly what makes the last half hour so hard to sit through.

Unannounced and wearing joke teeth, a shambolic German father turns up in Bucharest to torment his consultant daughter through an invented alter ego. It runs nearly three hours and uses them, building to an excruciating set piece that also happens to be the most humane thing in it.

A secretive team in Cardiff collects alien technology falling through a rift in time and space, answering to nobody and burying what it cannot explain. It begins as a laddish adult spin-off from Doctor Who, then with the five-night Children of Earth becomes something far bleaker and much better.

Bored with his life, a construction worker buys an implanted memory of a holiday on Mars and wakes up hunted by people who insist he is someone else entirely. Verhoeven plays the dream-or-reality question straight while smuggling in satire and a startling amount of gore.

A distracted fund manager takes his young daughter on the KTX from Seoul to Busan just as an infection tears through the country, trapping them carriage by carriage. The class satire is blunt, but the staging is superb and the sentiment is earned rather than assumed.

Operatives from a ruined future overwrite the minds of present-day people at the moment of their recorded deaths, then have to hold down the host's job, marriage and children between missions. The domestic mess is the real subject, and the show is far smarter about it than the premise suggests.

A fourteen-year-old girl hires a drunken, one-eyed marshal to hunt down the man who shot her father, and insists on riding along to watch it done. The Coens play the Western dead straight and let the period diction carry the comedy; Steinfeld's flat, unimpressed delivery holds the whole thing.

Long retired from killing and failing at pig farming, a widower takes one last bounty on two cowboys who cut a prostitute's face. Eastwood spends the film dismantling the myth he built a career on, and Hackman's genial, house-proud sheriff is the nastiest thing in it.

Two London detectives reopen cold cases when remains surface decades later, then pick apart the ordinary present-day lives of the handful of people who have spent years not thinking about it. The procedural is almost beside the point; it is a show about what guilt does to a quiet life.

A family's summer beach holiday is interrupted by four strangers standing silently in the driveway who look exactly like them. Peele's follow-up to Get Out is wilder and more ambitious, and the mythology does not entirely hold up; Nyong'o's double performance absolutely does.

The Vice President of the United States and her staff spend their days managing crises entirely of their own making, none of which matter to anyone outside the room. Iannucci's insult-writing is the best on television, and the later seasons under David Mandel get meaner as the satire curdles.

A brusque, rumpled DCI in a battered hat works murders across Northumberland, bullying her team affectionately through each case and going home alone to her father's house. Feature-length and formulaic by design; Blethyn and the bleak northern coastline are the entire appeal, and they are enough.

Forced into retirement by his fear of heights, a San Francisco detective is hired to follow an old friend's wife and becomes obsessed with her. Hitchcock's coldest and strangest film, less a thriller than a study of a man remaking a woman into an image he prefers.

A restless Norse farmer defies his chieftain to sail west and raid England, and the saga follows him and then his sons across decades of expansion and succession. Terrific in its early years when it stays close to the politics of one settlement; it thins out badly once the map widens.

The deadpan elder Addams daughter is shipped off to a boarding school for outcasts, where she investigates a series of killings nobody else will take seriously. Ortega's performance is the entire engine, and the teen-mystery plotting built around her is far more conventional than the character deserves.

A polished, promotion-chasing DI is handed a resentful East End murder squad and a case that copies the Ripper killings street by street. Each series takes on a different historical crime; the first is much the best, and Steve Pemberton's twitchy police historian is the reason to stay.

An elderly professor drives across Sweden to collect an honorary degree, and the journey keeps stalling into dreams and memories of everyone he has been cold to. Bergman at his warmest, with the silent-era director Victor Sjöström giving the central face its entire history for free.

On a Wyoming reservation, a wildlife tracker finds a young woman dead in the snow and helps a badly out-of-her-depth FBI agent work out how she got there. Sheridan is far better on the specifics of place, cold and jurisdiction than on the outsider's-eye framing he keeps returning to.

A respected New Orleans judge discovers his teenage son caused a fatal hit-and-run, and that the boy he killed belonged to a crime family. Cranston is excellent at watching a decent man choose wrong over and over; the second season stretches a premise that had already run its course.
